chunks: "A chip has several different kinds of circuits and they want different voltages, so a single supply is either wasteful or can't work at all. The main reason is power.
Dynamic power goes with V squared, so any block that doesn't need peak speed should run at a lower voltage.
A simple example: if 70% of the logic is not timing critical and can run at 0. 8 volts while 30% needs 1. 0 volts, dynamic power falls from 1. 0 to about 0. 75, a 25% saving.
In practice that means separate voltage domains for the big CPU cores, the little cores, the GPU and so on, each with its own DVFS, so each follows its own workload.
Second, different circuits have different needs. SRAM needs a higher minimum voltage than logic to stay stable, so it often sits on its own rail.
I/O has to match external standards, like 1. 8 volts or 3. 3 volts signaling, while the core runs near 0. 8 volts and uses thick-oxide I/O transistors.
Analog blocks like PLLs and ADCs want a clean, separate supply. Flash programming or LCD drivers need higher voltages.
And an always-on domain for the RTC and wake logic sits on its own rail so the rest of the chip can be switched off completely. The costs are real.
You need more regulators or a PMIC, board area and decoupling, a power-up sequence, level shifters wherever signals cross domains, and isolation cells when a domain is powered down.
And the regulator efficiency matters: a linear regulator dropping from 1. 0 to 0. 8 volts only saves 20% at the input, while a buck converter saves much more."
